children.text:
I am no lawyer but I am law-curious, so I went looking for more info on rangeCheck. As we all know AI erases liability, but I'm a poor old human still trying to compete with AI and I do have legal liability so I guess I still have to think about what the rules mean, eh?

Here's my thing: Oracle v Google was a fight that ended up being about two specific things, one was whether API-declaring interface code could be a subject of copyright law. Once it was found that interfaces could be copyrighted the lawsuit turned its focus to thing two: whether Google's use was fair use.

The part of copyright law, as written, that protects your ability to copy a 9-line RangeCheck function, is NOT, emphatically NOT fair use. It is convergence, the least-known of all the copyright principles.

Convergence says that if many people not coordinating could be expected to all land on the same results, then logically the activity must not be creative expression and the result must not be possible to copyright. This is why nobody owns math equations like e=mc^2. It's not that no creativity was required to derive the equation, it's that anyone working at it would end up with a result of that form.

In programming this would protect you when you do something like write a parser for a programming language, or implement a common helper function. Anything where you may, through now fault of your own, do work that creates a result similar to work that someone else has already done.

I don't know that any significant court case has ever even had arguments based on convergence even though it's the most practical shield most of us have most of the time.

Trivial has to be pretty trivial. Google was found by a jury to have infringed Oracle's copyright on 9 lines of source code (the RangeCheck function). Although that fact did get lost in surrounding rulings and appeals relating to a further 11,500 lines of API declarations. The legal criteria for what's trivial is subjective and not well defined at all. And the legal costs for finding out what is or is not trivial can easily run into millions of dollars.

If I were you, I would not copy even truly "trivial" amounts of code.
If the code is trivial, not copyrightable, you do not have to follow the license.

Um, no... MIT requires that the license text be included. That's attribution, because you normally put your name or the name of your organization in there. You can't just take MIT code and have AI rewrite it without attribution, at least, you need to do some kind of air gap or something, and lawyers might poke holes in that too. I'm sure people are doing it though. But GPL won't save you from that.

But I do understand why they want to move to GPL, to block out scammers who want to make closed-source forks and charge money for them.

> If that LLM […] didn’t have web search or access to the copy-left repo, […]

> Even if that model has been trained on that copy left code

How can an LLM be trained on code that it doesn’t have access to?

> cloning it is reverse engineering according to the courts.

What courts? Has there been any court case on this w.r.t. LLMs?

AFAIK, learning from copyrighted material is fine, copying copyrighted material (with some exceptions) isn’t. Where one ends and the other starts is a gray area, but at the far end of that scale lies learning by head and then reproducing verbatim. That definitely is copyright infringement.

Also, claiming “clean lab” isn’t worth much. Question is whether that holds up in court.

I would guess/hope/think one need not go as far as Phoenix technologies went to make a BIOS (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean-room_design), but I can see why they did things that way to be on the safe side.

But a lot of these reverse engineered projects claim “clean lab.” If that LLM was only given documents and didn’t have web search or access to the copy-left repo, cloning it is reverse engineering according to the courts.

Even if that model has been trained on that copy left code.

By that logic, anybody who's learned operating systems development via the book Operating Systems: Design and Implementation (Tanenbaum and Woodhull) would be legally unable to write an operating system, ever. That book had Minix source code, which at the time was, nevermind copyleft, proprietary.

AIUI this includes Linus Torvalds, and would have affected Linux. Which, by the way, is heavily written by LLM these days, including by Linus himself using Anthropic's tools.

An LLM reading some code and learning from it (at any point in time, in training or as used through agentic programming tools) is in this regard no different from an human being doing the same thing.

Nothing stops me from reading Asahi's source code and then writing my own from what I learned. My agent can do the same thing faster and better. It would also be less likely to resemble Asahi's, as an LLM has seen and learned from a far larger body of code than I have in my entire 30+ years of programming.

If anything, code is becoming no longer a product but a commodity, which brings us closer to the sort of freedom GNU and the FSF aimed for; Something to celebrate.

No, there's no way the genie is going back into the bottle. The past is not coming back. Reality is best accepted and worked with, not fought.

If the LLM has ‘seen’ the GPL-licensed code, it is debatable whether a reimplementation by that LLM is from scratch.

It doesn’t help the “yes it is; the LLM learned from reading that code, but didn’t copy it” camp that there have been cases where an LLM output blocks of code that are very similar to parts of GPL-licensed source code.

Question for copyright to apply then is whether those blocks are copyrightable and if so, whether the ‘copied’ text is similar enough to the source text.

Expand on "license laundering". How is a from-scratch re-implementation connected in any way? There's no code in common.

And the hardware the drivers are for is Apple's, not Asahi's, to begin with.
... which matches the definition of lincense laundering and is independent from the original license.
